episode_title: Patents, SPCs, UPC: how generic medicines reach the market (Jiri Slavik) | Talk IP to me Ep. 12

real_qa.q: What is the Unified Patent Court (UPC) and how does it affect generic pharmaceutical companies?
real_qa.r: The UPC is a new court system valid in certain European Patent Office contracting states but not all EPO member states. Generic companies face a significant challenge: the UPC operates on an opt-out regime where patent holders decide whether their patents are in the system, and most major pharma companies have opted out their main patents. Generic companies cannot unilaterally opt patents back in—only patent holders can. This means generic companies are often unable to file invalidation actions if patents are not opted into the UPC system, even though they can be sued there.
real_qa.requete: Unified Patent Court UPC generic pharma opt-out regime

real_qa.q: How do generic pharmaceutical companies navigate patent landscapes when planning products 5-10 years ahead?
real_qa.r: Generic companies must conduct IP landscaping from the beginning of product development to identify what patents cover a molecule, determine the earliest market entry date, and plan how to circumvent patents. IP is involved from start to finish—from initial planning through development, regulatory steps, and market launch. The challenge is that the IP landscape constantly changes through patent applications, grants, lapses, revocations, and appeals, making planning extremely difficult when looking 5-10 years into the future with an unknowable legal and regulatory environment.
real_qa.requete: generic pharma product development IP landscaping planning process

real_qa.q: What is the difference between generic drugs and value-added generic products in pharmaceuticals?
real_qa.r: A generic product has the same pharmaceutical dosage form and API as the innovator product. However, value-added generics bring additional benefit by modifying the formulation—for example, converting tablets into oral solutions, reducing pill burden from three pills to one per day, or offering different dosage forms that innovators no longer produce. Generic companies can leverage the innovator's clinical trial data after exclusivity ends while providing incremental innovations that create high patient value.
real_qa.requete: generic drug vs value-added generic pharmaceutical definition

real_qa.q: Why are Supplementary Protection Certificates (SPCs) granted for pharmaceutical patents?
real_qa.r: Patents provide 20 years of protection, but pharmaceutical companies must file patents early in development before lengthy clinical trials and regulatory approval. SPCs extend exclusivity by approximately 5 to 5.5 years, resulting in roughly 15 years total exclusivity from market launch. SPCs exist because companies cannot enjoy patent protection benefits until they actually commercialize the product, so SPCs compensate for the time lost to development and regulatory approval processes.
real_qa.requete: Supplementary Protection Certificates SPC pharmaceutical patents why allowed

real_qa.q: What was the public access to documents case at the UPC involving Chris Fothers?
real_qa.r: Chris Fothers, named one of the most influential people in IP in 2024, filed a public access to documents request at the UPC. The case reached the Court of Appeal stage where he required legal representation. Yiris Lovic, along with a group of interested attorneys, represented Fothers in this case, which was influential and reached the appellate level. It addressed an important issue for the new UPC court regarding transparency and public access to documents—an area that Lovic had been closely following since the UPC's inception.
real_qa.requete: Chris Fothers UPC public access documents case Court of Appeal

guest.titre: Czech and European Patent Attorney, UPC Representative, IP Leader
guest.bio_context: Yiris Lovic studied organic chemistry at university in Prague and specialized secondary chemistry education. He began as a junior patent specialist at a well-known pharmaceutical company after graduation, knowing nothing about patent work initially, but continued formal education through a two-year IP course at the IP office and European Patent Attorney (EQE) exams. He has worked in-house in pharma for over 10 years while building IP Duo, a patent attorney practice focused on pharma, biotech, and patent litigation at the intersection of these fields.
